clue.text: Somehow narrate in book the author's name

indicators.note: somehow means in some way or other, telling us these three words are to be rearranged in some fashion

explanation.surface: An instruction to tell a story inside a book that carries its writer's name on the cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' signals that all thirteen letters of NARRATE, IN and BOOK are rearranged; the result is the name of the Booker-winning novelist of Hotel du Lac.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita Brookner was an English novelist and art historian, so her full name is a writer's name.

clue.text: Shute's place comparable to Bailey novel

parts.note: a town is a place where people live
something comparable to another is like it
Alice (1994) is a novel by the critic John Bayley, whose name the clue spells Bailey

explanation.surface: A remark comparing a setting in Nevil Shute's fiction with a book by a writer called Bailey.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist behind Alice is John Bayley, Iris Murdoch's husband; the clue's spelling Bailey is either the setter's or the printer's. 'Shute's' alone defines: the answer is the title of Nevil Shute's 1950 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevil Shute wrote the 1950 novel of that title, set partly in the Australian outback town of Alice Springs.

clue.text: End of book found in blind experimentalism

indicators.note: found in says the letters needed sit inside the words that follow, across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A reviewer complains that the last pages of a book are full of unseeing avant-garde experiment.
explanation.definitionFit: An alphabetical list of names and topics with page references normally comes at the back of a book.

clue.text: A case for being objective

parts.note: reads like a plea for impartiality, but the grammatical case is meant: the one used for the object of a verb

explanation.surface: Someone argues in favour of impartial judgement.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the case that marks the direct object of a verb is also called the objective case.

clue.text: Again makes accessible revised letters of Penrose Source of Upton Sinclair's inspiration in 1927

indicators.note: the letters of the name are revised, that is, put into a new order

explanation.surface: A notice that the Penrose collection's letters have been revised and the archive is open again.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held carries the text of the clue for 5-down tacked onto its end; those words play no part here. 'revised letters of' rearranges PENROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that opens once more makes a place or thing available again after a closure.

clue.text: Source of Upton Sinclair's inspiration in 1927

definitions.text: Source of Upton Sinclair's inspiration in 1927

parts.words: Source of Upton Sinclair's inspiration in 1927
parts.note: Upton Sinclair's 1927 novel was called Oil!, so the source of its inspiration is read literally as the place crude oil comes from

explanation.surface: A literary question about what prompted an American novelist's 1927 book.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair's novel Oil! drew on the California petroleum boom, and a drilled shaft is the source of petroleum.

clue.text: Christie's fatal river

parts.note: points to Agatha Christie's novel Death on the ... , whose title names an African river

explanation.surface: A river that proved deadly in an Agatha Christie mystery.
explanation.definitionFit: Christie's 1937 mystery Death on the Nile is set on a steamer cruising Egypt's great river.

clue.text: Storey book suggests Gothic novelist

explanation.surface: A novel by David Storey hints at an author of Gothic romances.
explanation.definitionFit: David Storey published the novel Radcliffe in 1963, and Ann Radcliffe wrote The Mysteries of Udolpho, a classic Gothic romance.

clue.text: Eponymous Australian con-man

parts.note: Peter Carey's novel Illywhacker takes its title from Australian slang for a trickster, and its narrator is that trickster

explanation.surface: A swindler from Australia who gives his name to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eponymous' is meant loosely: the narrator of Carey's Illywhacker is the illywhacker (Australian slang for a confidence man) of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of Peter Carey's 1985 novel Illywhacker is a lying trickster, the illywhacker or swindler the title names.

clue.text: Dotheboys Hall, for instance — hardly a draw, but might be a tie

definitions.text: Dotheboys Hall, for instance — hardly a draw, but might be a tie

parts.words: Dotheboys Hall, for instance — hardly a draw, but might be a tie
parts.note: Dotheboys Hall is Squeers's academy in Nicholas Nickleby, an establishment of the traditional kind; 'tie' suggests a sporting result but means the striped neckwear worn by former pupils

explanation.surface: Dickens's grim Yorkshire academy is hardly attractive, yet it could end level in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' and 'tie' both look like match results; 'hardly a draw' says no-one would be attracted to Dickens's brutal school, while the 'tie' is the neckwear of former pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotheboys Hall is a school of the traditional sort, and old boys wear a striped tie marking their former school.

clue.text: Put up a novelist

explanation.surface: Someone gives a bed for the night to a writer of fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone up is to give them a room for the night, and David Lodge is the English novelist of Small World and Nice Work.

clue.text: Henry Miller's bond

explanation.surface: A tie or attachment belonging to the American writer Henry Miller.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Miller's novel Nexus closes his Rosy Crucifixion trilogy, and the word itself means a connecting link or tie.

clue.text: Garden writer from New Zealand

explanation.surface: A gardening columnist who comes from New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise in Genesis is a garden, and Dorothy Eden was a New Zealand-born writer of romantic suspense novels.

clue.text: Nash thought the English belonged to the most exclusive one

definitions.text: Nash thought the English belonged to the most exclusive one

parts.words: Nash thought the English belonged to the most exclusive one
parts.note: Ogden Nash wrote that every Englishman is convinced that being English means belonging to the most exclusive association there is

explanation.surface: A remark by the American poet Ogden Nash about English snobbery.
explanation.definitionFit: In his poem England Expects, Ogden Nash says being English is membership of the most exclusive society of all.

clue.text: Scots poet beyond criticism

parts.note: praise for a poet with no faults, turned round: this Dundee poet was so bad that criticism could not reach him

explanation.surface: A Scottish poet whose work is too good to fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beyond criticism' sounds like high praise; it means the opposite, since William McGonagall is famous as the worst poet in English.
explanation.definitionFit: William McGonagall of Dundee, author of The Tay Bridge Disaster, is celebrated for verse so bad it disarms critics.

clue.text: King of Lycia, wandering friend of Zeus, and Fagin's pupil

parts.note: Io, loved by Zeus, was turned into a heifer and roamed the world chased by a gadfly
Charley Bates is one of Fagin's young pickpockets in Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: A list of three figures: a Lycian monarch, a roving lover of Zeus and a boy thief from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists three people, but only the first defines; the other two are the pieces. Charley Bates is the Artful Dodger's companion in Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Lycian ruler Iobates set Bellerophon to kill the Chimera.

clue.text: It offers support to all writers

definitions.text: It offers support to all writers

parts.words: It offers support to all writers
parts.note: sounds like a fund or charity for authors, but the support is physical: a ledge that holds up their volumes

explanation.surface: A grant scheme that helps every author.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelf for books holds up the works of every author on it, physically supporting them.

clue.text: A match for Milton's demon of Sinful Pride

explanation.surface: Milton's proud fallen angel meets his equal.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucifer was an early friction match, and in Paradise Lost the rebel archangel is Satan, once named for the morning star.

clue.text: Developed, like Darwin's endless forms most beautiful

definitions.text: like Darwin's endless forms most beautiful

explanation.surface: Something grew in the manner of the many lovely species Darwin wrote of.
explanation.definitionFit: Developed means grew gradually; On the Origin of Species ends saying endless forms most beautiful have been, and are being, brought about this way.

clue.text: Epitome of renaissance man

parts.note: a person of many talents is called a renaissance man, and the Florentine painter, engineer and inventor is its prime example

explanation.surface: The perfect example of a many-talented person.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo, painter of the Mona Lisa and designer of flying machines, is the standard example of the all-round genius.

clue.text: In favour of part of speech showing potted wisdom

parts.note: pro means for or in favour of
a verb is one of the parts of speech

explanation.surface: Someone backs a grammatical category that displays pithy common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A saying such as a stitch in time saves nine is a short traditional maxim, wisdom compressed into a sentence.

clue.text: Tag rag, merry derry, — and hatband!" (John O'Keeffe)

definitions.text: Tag rag, merry derry, — and hatband!" (John O'Keeffe)

parts.words: Tag rag, merry derry, — and hatband!" (John O'Keeffe)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from the Irish playwright John O'Keeffe: the dash stands for a wig in the line

explanation.surface: A line of comic nonsense verse from the playwright John O'Keeffe with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in clue: the missing word in O'Keeffe's line is the name of a fashionable eighteenth-century wig.
explanation.definitionFit: The line runs Tag rag, merry derry, periwig and hatband, the missing word being an old powdered wig.

clue.text: Evelyn Waugh's final character

parts.note: Tony, hero of Waugh's A Handful of Dust, has a surname meaning final

explanation.surface: The last figure Evelyn Waugh created.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks as if it asks for the last character Waugh wrote; instead 'final' gives the surname of Tony, hero of A Handful of Dust.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Last is the hero of Waugh's A Handful of Dust, and his surname means final.

clue.text: Always part of creative verisimilitude

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A writer insists that invented realism is a constant need.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever, as in 'ever hopeful', means at all times, constantly.

clue.text: "And I have to be / Where no storms come" (G. M. Hopkins)

definitions.text: "And I have to be / Where no storms come" (G. M. Hopkins)

parts.words: "And I have to be / Where no storms come" (G. M. Hopkins)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Hopkins's poem Heaven-Haven, a nun's wish for a calm place; the gap is a verb of requesting

explanation.surface: Lines from Hopkins's Heaven-Haven with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in clue: in Heaven-Haven the nun says she has requested to be where no storms come.
explanation.definitionFit: The line reads And I have asked to be, a past participle meaning requested.

clue.text: First Kurosawa, of the "original Western", makes obeisance

indicators.note: first applies to every word that follows: take the opening letter of each

explanation.surface: Kurosawa, maker of the film that inspired the first spaghetti Western, receives a respectful bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' takes the opening letter of each of the next five words. KOTOW is an older spelling of kowtow, to bow with the forehead to the ground; the definition reads as a verb in the third person.
explanation.definitionFit: To kowtow is to kneel and touch the ground with one's head in deep respect, a gesture of homage.

clue.text: Making train run on time an early achievement of Nobel Prize winner

definitions.text: Making train run on time an early achievement of Nobel Prize winner

parts.words: Making train run on time an early achievement of Nobel Prize winner
parts.note: looks like railway efficiency, but refers to the early novella The Train Was on Time by a German Nobel laureate

explanation.surface: A future Nobel laureate first won fame by getting the trains to run punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: Heinrich Böll's first published book (1949) was The Train Was on Time; he won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1972. The grid drops the umlaut.
explanation.definitionFit: The German writer Heinrich Böll, Nobel laureate in 1972, began his career with the novella The Train Was on Time.

clue.text: Belief in Mozart mass

explanation.surface: Faith expressed through a Mass by Mozart.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement of faith, and Mozart's Mass in C, K257, is nicknamed the Credo Mass.

clue.text: The best sun we have was made of its coal, Walpole thought

definitions.text: The best sun we have was made of its coal, Walpole thought

parts.words: The best sun we have was made of its coal, Walpole thought
parts.note: Horace Walpole joked about the grey English climate that the best sun the English had came from burning coal from the Tyneside port

explanation.surface: Horace Walpole's quip that English sunshine comes from a coal fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace Walpole wrote that 'the best sun we have is made of Newcastle coal'; the Tyneside city was Britain's great coal port.
explanation.definitionFit: The city on the Tyne shipped coal across Britain, which Walpole said gave the only reliable sunshine in England.
